body_html:
How long does an insurance appraisal take? Most residential property appraisals in Texas wrap up in about 4 to 12 weeks from the written demand to a signed award. Simple roof claims can finish in under a month; large fire, structural, or commercial losses that need an umpire often take three to six months.

When a claim stalls, time feels personal. Every week of delay affects repairs, living arrangements, and cash flow. The good news is that appraisal is usually far faster than litigation, and much of the timeline is within your control.

Below, we break down each stage of the appraisal process, realistic durations for different claim types, the Texas-specific deadlines that shape the schedule, and practical steps that keep things moving.

Insurance appraisal timeline at a glance

Every claim is different, but these ranges reflect how long an insurance appraisal typically takes for common property losses when both sides participate in good faith:

Claim typeTypical appraisal timeline
Small residential loss (single roof or interior room)2–4 weeks
Moderate home damage (roof plus interior, multiple trades)4–8 weeks
Large or complex residential loss (fire, structural)2–4 months
Umpire required or heavily disputed claim3–6 months
Commercial or multi-unit property3–6+ months

These are working estimates, not promises. Appraisals move at the speed of people, documents, and cooperation, which is why two hail claims on the same street can finish weeks apart.

What is an insurance appraisal, and why does timing vary?

A property insurance appraisal is not a real estate appraisal. It does not set market value. It resolves a disagreement over the amount of loss on a claim, using a process written into most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies.

Each side names its own appraiser. The two appraisers try to agree on the amount of loss. If they cannot, a neutral umpire decides the disputed items, and an award signed by any two of the three is generally binding on the amount. Read our full explainer on what an insurance appraisal is for the basics.

Timing varies because the process has several hand-offs: invoking, appointing, inspecting, estimating, negotiating, and sometimes umpiring. A delay at any hand-off pushes everything else back.

How long does each stage of the appraisal process take?

Here is where the time actually goes, stage by stage.

1. Invoking the appraisal clause (day 1)

Appraisal starts with a written demand from you or the insurer. The letter identifies the claim, states that you disagree on the amount of loss, and invokes the appraisal provision. This step takes a day once you decide to proceed. See what happens after invoking the appraisal clause in Texas for the details.

2. Appointing appraisers (up to about 20 days)

Many Texas policies give each side 20 days after the written demand to name a competent, disinterested appraiser. If you hire your appraiser before you send the demand, your side is ready on day one. Carriers sometimes use the full window.

3. Selecting an umpire (often 15 days, sometimes longer)

The two appraisers then try to agree on an umpire, often within 15 days under typical policy language. If they cannot agree, either side can usually ask a Texas court to appoint one, which can add several weeks. Some appraisers agree on an umpire early even if they expect to settle without one. Learn more about how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas.

4. Property inspection (1–3 weeks)

Both appraisers inspect the property, ideally together. Scheduling depends on access, weather, roof safety, and the size of the loss. Complex claims may need a second visit, an engineer, or a specialty trade such as HVAC or electrical.

5. Estimate preparation (1–4 weeks)

Each appraiser builds or refines a line-item estimate, usually in Xactimate or Symbility. This is where scope differences, pricing, code upgrades, overhead and profit, and repair-versus-replace questions come into focus. Simple roof estimates may take a week; whole-house fire estimates take much longer.

6. Appraiser negotiations (1–6 weeks)

The appraisers compare estimates line by line and try to reach agreement. Cooperative, well-documented files often settle in a week or two. Contentious files with large gaps can take a month or more.

7. Umpire review, if needed (2–6 additional weeks)

When items remain in dispute, the umpire reviews both estimates and the evidence, may inspect the property, and decides the disputed amounts. This adds time, but it also ends the stalemate.

8. Signed award (a few days)

Once two of the three panel members agree, they sign the appraisal award and deliver it to both parties. This last step is usually quick.

How long after the appraisal award will insurance pay?

Payment timing depends on your policy and the carrier, but in Texas, many insurers issue payment within days to a few weeks after receiving the signed award. Chapter 542 of the Texas Insurance Code generally requires an insurer to pay an accepted claim within 5 business days after notifying the policyholder that it will pay.

Payment can take longer when:

  • A mortgage company must be named on the check and endorse it
  • Recoverable depreciation is held back until repairs are completed
  • Prior payments must be deducted and the award reconciled
  • The carrier disputes coverage for part of the award

Use our Texas claim deadline calculator to estimate prompt-payment dates,. If depreciation was withheld, ask your appraiser how much may be released once repairs are done. Courts have held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically end every prompt-payment claim, but that area of law is nuanced; this is general information, not legal advice.

What makes an insurance appraisal take longer?

Time is rarely lost on site. It is lost between emails. These are the most common reasons an insurance appraisal takes longer than expected:

  • Incomplete documentation: missing photos, receipts, or prior estimates slow every stage.
  • Late appraiser appointment: waiting to hire your appraiser until after the demand burns weeks.
  • Umpire disputes: disagreement over who the umpire should be can require court appointment.
  • Catastrophe backlogs: after a major Texas hail or hurricane event, every adjuster, appraiser, and contractor is busy.
  • Complex scope: code upgrades, matching issues, engineering questions, and multiple trades add analysis time.
  • Coverage disputes: appraisal decides amount of loss, not coverage, so a parallel coverage argument can stall things.

And these factors speed things up:

  • Hiring an experienced appraiser early
  • Organized photos, video, and a clear damage timeline
  • Prompt responses to inspection and document requests
  • Appraisers who know Texas pricing and the local building codes
Tip: Before invoking appraisal, gather the carrier's estimate, your contractor's estimate, every photo, and all correspondence in one folder. Label everything by date so both appraisers can find it quickly.

Insurance appraisal timelines in Texas

Texas has more hail claims than any other state, and spring storm seasons in Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio, and the Panhandle can produce thousands of claims in a single week. Hurricanes on the Gulf Coast do the same for Houston, Galveston, and Corpus Christi. Those surges stretch every part of the appraisal timeline.

Texas-specific factors that affect how long an insurance appraisal takes include:

  • Policy deadlines: many Texas policies use 20 days to name appraisers and 15 days to agree on an umpire.
  • Court-appointed umpires: if appraisers deadlock, a judge in the county where the property sits may appoint the umpire.
  • Chapter 542A: weather claims headed toward litigation carry a 61-day pre-suit notice requirement, which can affect strategy and sequencing.
  • Binding awards: Texas courts generally enforce appraisal awards on the amount of loss, so the time you invest usually produces a final number.

Our appraisers work across the state, including Dallas and Houston, and track these deadlines on every file.

Simple vs. complex property appraisals

The single biggest predictor of appraisal time is complexity. Compare these scenarios:

ScenarioExpected timelineWhy
Hail-damaged shingle roof only2–4 weeksOne trade, measurable scope
Roof plus interior water damage4–6 weeksMultiple trades, drying and mold questions
Kitchen or whole-house fire2–4 monthsSmoke, contents, code upgrades
Structural or foundation-related loss3–6 monthsEngineering reports, causation questions
Apartment complex or commercial building3–6+ monthsMany units, systems, and stakeholders

If your claim involves engineers, many trades, or code upgrades, a longer schedule is normal. Careful work on a large loss is worth the extra weeks.

How homeowners can keep the appraisal moving

You cannot control the carrier, but you can control your side of the file:

  1. Hire your appraiser before you invoke. This removes the first delay entirely.
  2. Provide evidence up front. Photos, video, estimates, invoices, and weather data. See what evidence helps during insurance appraisal.
  3. Be available for inspections. Offer several dates and make sure the roof and interior are accessible.
  4. Do not invoke too late. Waiting months in stalled negotiations only adds time.
  5. Keep communication centralized. Route questions through your appraiser so nothing falls through the cracks.

Is an insurance appraisal worth the time?

Appraisal is not just about speed. It is about getting to a resolution. It is often worth the wait when:

  • The gap between your estimate and the carrier's is significant
  • Negotiations and supplements have stalled
  • Repairs are on hold because the payment will not cover them
  • You want a binding number without the cost and years of a lawsuit

It helps to compare the likely cost of appraisal against the amount in dispute. For a broader view of each phase, see the insurance appraisal timeline explained.

Next steps: setting realistic expectations

So, how long does an insurance appraisal take? For most Texas homeowners, plan on one to three months, with simple roof claims often finishing faster and complex or umpired losses taking longer. Payment typically follows within days to a few weeks of the signed award.

The key is not rushing the process but managing it well: an early appraiser, organized evidence, and steady follow-through. Done right, appraisal brings a stalled claim to a clear, final number much sooner than the alternatives.

faqs.q: How long does appraisal take for a home insurance claim?
faqs.a: Most home insurance appraisals take roughly four to twelve weeks from the written demand to a signed award. A straightforward roof claim may resolve in two to four weeks, while fire, structural, or heavily disputed claims that require an umpire can take three to six months. Documentation, scheduling, and catastrophe backlogs drive most of the variation.

faqs.q: How long after an appraisal award does the insurance company pay?
faqs.a: Many Texas insurers pay within days to a few weeks after receiving a signed appraisal award. Texas prompt-payment law generally requires payment within five business days after the insurer notifies you it will pay. Mortgage company endorsements, held-back recoverable depreciation, and offsets for prior payments can extend the time before funds are fully in hand.

faqs.q: Does adding an umpire make appraisal take longer?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. When the two appraisers cannot agree, the umpire must review both estimates and the evidence and may inspect the property, which often adds two to six weeks. If the appraisers cannot even agree on who the umpire should be, a court appointment in Texas can add more time before the review begins.

faqs.q: Can I start repairs while the appraisal is in progress?
faqs.a: Often you can, especially to prevent further damage, but talk with your appraiser first. Both appraisers need a fair chance to inspect and document the damage before it is removed. Thorough photos, video, and saved samples help preserve evidence if repairs must begin before inspections are complete.

faqs.q: Is appraisal faster than suing the insurance company?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Appraisal typically resolves an amount-of-loss dispute in weeks or a few months, while property insurance lawsuits commonly take a year or more and cost considerably more. Appraisal does not decide coverage questions, however, so some disputes still require legal advice from a Texas attorney.
